name: FAIR Data
title: FAIR Data
answer: FAIR Data is a set of guiding principles for making research data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable, published in 2016 and now widely adopted across research funders, journals and repositories. It applies to data as well as to the metadata that describes it, and it covers the whole lifecycle from collection through deposit, citation and long term preservation. In practice it is less a technical standard than a shared expectation about how datasets should be described, identified and kept usable by people and machines alike. It sits alongside open data policy but is not identical to it, since data can be FAIR while remaining access controlled.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: FAIR Data is a set of guiding principles for making research data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable, published in 2016 and now widely adopted across research funders, journals and repositories. It applies to data as well as to the metadata that describes it, and it covers the whole lifecycle from collection through deposit, citation and long term preservation. In practice it is less a technical standard than a shared expectation about how datasets should be described, identified and kept usable by people and machines alike. It sits alongside open data policy but is not identical to it, since data can be FAIR while remaining access controlled.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: FAIR data runs on persistent identifiers such as DOIs, structured metadata schemas, and repository platforms that expose machine readable records through APIs. Discipline specific repositories and generalist ones both play a role, and controlled vocabularies and ontologies supply the shared terms that make records comparable across collections. Storage, backup and preservation layers sit underneath, often in institutional or national infrastructure, and provenance tracking records where a dataset came from and how it has changed. The site's own library of 295 research papers and 14104 extracted claims illustrates the same pattern of structured records pointing back to original sources rather than to summaries.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts at planning, when a researcher decides what will be captured, in what format, and under what licence, then continues through documentation, naming conventions and version control during the project. On deposit, the dataset is assigned a persistent identifier and described with metadata that names variables, units, methods and any conditions of access. Reviewers and data stewards check that records meet repository requirements, and citations link publications to the datasets behind them. Because the site links to original papers rather than to a search tool, the same habit applies here: the record points to the source, and the reader follows it.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on consent, privacy, licensing and the limits of what can be shared, especially with human subject data, Indigenous data and commercially sensitive material. Access levels, embargoes and data use agreements let a dataset be findable without being openly downloadable, and licences such as Creative Commons variants set out what reuse is permitted. Provenance matters for trust, since a record should show who created the data, under what conditions, and whether it has been corrected or withdrawn. Institutions, funders and repositories each carry part of the responsibility, and the practical questions are usually about disclosure risk and attribution rather than about the principles themselves.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Work is moving toward automated metadata generation, richer provenance graphs and better links between datasets, code and publications, with AI tools increasingly used to draft and check records. Funders and journals continue to tighten requirements, and machine actionability, meaning data that software can use without human interpretation, is becoming a common expectation rather than an aspiration. Persistent identifiers and citation practice are spreading into more fields, and training for researchers is shifting from optional to routine. The open questions are less about whether FAIR will be adopted than about who pays for stewardship over the long term and how access controls and openness are balanced.
